questions.q: If the derivative of the function $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}b x^2+a x+4 ; & x \geq-1 \\ a x^2+b ; & x \lt  -1\end{array}\right.$ is everywhere continuous, then
questions.solution:
The function $f(x)$ is defined as $f(x) = bx^2 + ax + 4$ for $x \geq -1$ and $f(x) = ax^2 + b$ for $x \lt -1$.

For the derivative $f'(x)$ to be continuous everywhere, $f(x)$ must be continuous at $x = -1$. Thus, $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}} f(x) = f(-1)$.

Calculating the limits: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} (ax^2 + b) = a + b$ and $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} (bx^2 + ax + 4) = b - a + 4$.

Equating these, $a + b = b - a + 4$, which simplifies to $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$.

Now, consider the derivative $f'(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{cc} 2bx + a; & x \gt -1 \\ 2ax; & x \lt -1 \end{array}\right\}$.

For $f'(x)$ to be continuous at $x = -1$, the left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative must be equal: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} f'(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}} f'(x)$.

Substituting $a = 2$: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} (2ax) = 2(2)(-1) = -4$.

The right-hand derivative is $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} (2bx + a) = 2b(-1) + 2 = -2b + 2$.

Equating these, $-4 = -2b + 2$, which gives $2b = 6$, so $b = 3$.

Thus, $a = 2$ and $b = 3$.

Answer: $a=2, b=3$

Statement $1 \lim _{x \rightarrow 0}[g(x) \cos x-g(0) \operatorname{cosec} x]=f^{\prime \prime}(0)$.
Statement $2 f^{\prime}(0)=g(0)$.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true
questions.solution:
We have,

\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{g(x) \cos x-g(0)}{\sin x} \\
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{g^{\prime}(x) \cos x-g(x) \sin x}{\cos x}=0
\end{aligned}

Since, $f(x)=g(x) \sin x$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x) \sin x+g(x) \cos x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime \prime}(x)=g^{\prime \prime}(x) \sin x+2 g^{\prime}(x) \cos x-g(x) \sin x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime \prime}(0)=0
\end{aligned}

Thus, $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}[g(x) \cos x-g(0) \operatorname{cosec} x]=0=f^{\prime \prime}(0)\Rightarrow$ Statement 1 is true.
Statement 2. $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x) \sin x+g(x) \cos x$
\Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(0)=g(0)

Statement 2 is not a correct explanation of Statement 1.
